Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and Honorable members of the Housing and Economic Development commitee.
My name is Deqa Dhalac, and I have the honor of serving the good people of District 120 in South Portland. I am writing today in strong support of LD 1287, a vital piece of legislation that will help advance housing stability and strengthen Maine's workforce.
The housing crisis in Maine, and particularly in South Portland, is deeply affecting families and workers. It is a key factor contributing to the labor shortage, as too many residents are struggling to secure stable housing. While long-term strategies are important, we also need immediate action to prevent further homelessness and offer critical support to those at risk.
According to the Maine Development Foundation, the state's labor force declined sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic. Although we've seen signs of recovery, challenges persist, especially as our population ages and younger workers face economic barriers. If we want to attract and retain a robust workforce, we must invest in housing solutions that make it possible for all Mainers to live and work here.
LD 1287 takes an essential step in that direction. It provides rental assistance to households earning less than 30% of the area median income--supporting those who are often excluded from traditional housing programs. By focusing on prevention of eviction, the bill helps reduce homelessness, stabilize families, and allow individuals to maintain employment and contribute to the economy.
In South Portland, we see every day how stable housing the foundation of a strong, reliable workforce is. This bill aligns with our shared economic goals by supporting workers who are essential to our communities but face growing housing insecurity.
The structure of LD 1287 is both compassionate and practical. By empowering the Maine State Housing Authority to work with local partners and by keeping administrative costs low, we can ensure that more resources go directly to the renters who need them most.
Programs like those proposed in LD 1287 have already shown great promise in Southern Maine and Androscoggin County, helping workers access housing through security deposits and short-term assistance. These efforts have made a real difference, and LD 1287 would build on that success statewide.

District 120: Part of South Portland

By passing this bill and creating the Housing Stability Support Program and Housing Stability Fund, we can help keep families in their homes, support our workforce, and strengthen Maine's economic future. Thank you for your time, leadership, and commitment to this important issue. Sincerely, Deqa Dhalac
District 120: Part of South Portland

10056848:
Testimony of Erik C. Jorgensen Senior Director of Government Relations & Communications Maine State Housing Authority
Before The Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development (132nd)
In support of LD 1287: An Act to Support Workforce Development
by Establishing the Housing Stability Fund
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development, I am Erik Jorgensen Senior Director of Government Relations and Communications at the Maine State Housing Authority (MaineHousing) and I am submitting this testimony in support of LD 1287 An Act to Support Workforce Development by Establishing the Housing Stability Fund.
MaineHousing has been helping Maine people own, rent, repair, and heat their homes since 1969. We are an independent state authority (not a state agency) created to address the problems of unsafe, unsuitable, overcrowded, and unaffordable housing. We are authorized to issue bonds to finance single family mortgages for first time homebuyers and for affordable multi-family housing.
We are also authorized to administer a number of state and federal programs, including rental subsidies, weatherization, fuel assistance, two housing block grants,
1

the low-income housing tax credit program, and homeless grant programs. We receive state general fund revenue for homeless programs and receive a dedicated portion of the real estate transfer tax for the Housing Opportunities for Maine (HOME) Fund.
LD 1287 is a bill that proposes to provide rental assistance for low income households payable to landlords in the amount of $300 per month up to a total per household of $3,000. Like LD 1522, which is also being heard today, it offers a potential solution to the difficult challenge of rental affordability, this one at a lower level of cost to the state than with the other bill. Many of the themes you will hear around both of these bills will be similar, and regardless of what your policy decision is concerning how much funding the legislature might provide, our experience has shown that rental assistance can be a valuable tool in reducing evictions and keeping people housed.
My understanding is that this bill builds on successful work completed under the 131st legislature's Emergency Housing Relief fund, and helps to bridge a gap between what a household can afford to pay, what other programs provide, and what the household owes for rent. Between 2023 and 2024, a version of this program was being operated in Southern Maine, serving a total of 240 low-income households who received security deposits, and 109 families who accessed shortterm rental assistance to serve as a bridge to employment and self-sufficiency. We understand that these households accessed an average of just 4 months of support. We know, therefore, that this is a concept that can work.
Whatever the best policy is really depends on both the priorities of this committee and the level of funding that is available. Rental affordability is a very difficult and real problem in Maine, and we do know that extremely low-income households in
2

our state (at or below 30% of area median income, which this bill focuses on) almost all face a severe housing cost burden. This means that they are spending more than 50% of their household income on direct housing costs (mostly rent). If funding becomes available, MaineHousing, who is named in the bill, would be willing and able to administer this program on behalf of the state. Thank you.

Testimony Neither For Nor Against
L.D. 1287, An Act to Support Workforce Development by Establishing the Housing Stability Fund
April 25, 2025
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development, the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future offers this testimony neither for nor against LD 1287, An Act to Support Workforce Development by Establishing the Housing Stability Fund.
While the acute lack of housing supply is a national problem, the Mills Administration has taken historic action to address it. Working in bipartisan fashion with Legislature, we have invested more than $314 million in proven affordable housing programs for renters and homeowners alike. Over 1,500 affordable housing units have been fully constructed, completed and occupied since Governor Mills took office, while more than 1,400 units are under construction and another 2,500+ are in the underwriting stage. This is the largest pipeline that MaineHousing has ever experienced in its more than 50-year history.
We have also taken a leadership role in addressing the zoning and land use restrictions that make it unnecessarily difficult for communities to add the additional homes that Maine people need. Homeowners are now adding accessory dwelling units for loved ones or to provide desperately needed rental units, while developers are utilizing the modest density increases authorized through bipartisan action taken in the 130th and 131st Legislature.
Furthermore, the Administration has worked closely with the Legislature to address the emergency housing needs of thousands of Maine people over the past several years, including support for winter warming shelters, the year-round shelter network, rapid rehousing initiatives and other programs that have provided short and long-term housing relief for those experiencing homelessness. We are particularly excited to see the bipartisan Home for Good Program, which will provide permanent supportive housing and 24/7 on-site services for people experiencing chronic homelessness, announce its first five awards for initiatives to be developed in Sanford, Portland, Augusta, Auburn and Bangor. That program has the potential to make Maine the first state in the nation to end chronic homelessness.
LD 1287 proposes to build upon recent, successful work creating housing stability for those with a clear path to financial independence, but who need short-term housing support to get there. Its strategic approach utilizes limited dollars to help support critical workforce participation.
Over the last two years and with less than $1.2 million, a total of 240 households received assistance with security deposits, and 109 families accessed short-term rental assistance using an average of just 4 months of support. These outcomes demonstrate the program's efficiency, strategic approach and targeted impact.

James Myall, Senior Policy Analyst April 30, 2025
Dear Senator Curry, Representative Gere and member of Joint Standing Housing and Economic Development Committee,
To aid the Committee in its deliberations on LD 1522, "An Act to Establish the Maine Eviction Prevention Program," the Maine Center for Economic Policy has attempted to quantify the public savings created by the Eviction Prevention Program in its pilot phase. While comprehensive data was not available in all areas, we hope this information will help to demonstrate the range of costs that can be avoided when individuals have stable housing. Because this analysis focuses on public costs, it does not quantify the full costs to families who are evicted, and the negative impacts it has on their lives. It also does not include the full range of less tangible social costs that come from housing insecurity.
While this analysis was inspired by LD 1522, it may also be useful in considering other housing assistance bills such as LD 1287, "An Act to Support Workforce Development by Establishing the Housing Stability Fund."
Please feel free to reach out to me at jmyall@mecep.org with questions about this analysis.

The Eviction Prevention Pilot Program is expected to serve 1,600 households over the pilot period at a cost of $18 million, equivalent to $11,250 per household.1
Since the program prioritizes individuals who are facing eviction, this analysis assumes that the program has a 100% success rate in preventing evictions.
To date, the 850 households served by the program represent 1,900 individuals,2 implying that the full 1,600 served households will represent 3,576 individuals.
General Assistance Costs
In many cases, the Eviction Prevention Program will be replacing General Assistance as a source of support for applicants. Unfortunately, there is no comprehensive data available on how many applicants to the EPP were receiving General Assistance at the time of their application, and how much their need for General Assistance was reduced as a result of participating in the program. However, it is potentially a significant amount. In Portland, for example, 59% of GA applicants received housing support vouchers in 2024.3 For Maine taxpayers, funding these needs through the state's general fund is generally better than using local property taxes, since general fund revenue is more progressive, and asks more from higher-income Mainers who can most afford it. In general, property taxes place a proportionally higher ask on Mainers with low and middle incomes.
Court Costs
Evictions create direct costs to the public court system. The fee charged to landlords from filing a Forcible Entry and Detainer Action in Maine court is only $100, which means that the remainder of the cost of adjudicating the case falls on the public purse. According to a Judicial Branch time management study, FED cases account for 528,477 of 25,224,195 minutes in staff time each year, or 1% of court personnel time.4 The Judicial Branch's operational expenses in 2024 totaled $79,790,115 in 2024,5 meaning that 1% of this cost represents $797,901. If the court collects $100 in fees from each of the 4,843 Forcible Entry cases filed each year, it raises $484,300 in offsetting revenue, for a net public cost of $313,601, or $65 per eviction filing. As an outside estimate, avoiding eviction filings for the $1,600 households in the EPP will save the judicial system $104,000 in costs each year.

Shelter Costs
Evictions increase the risk of homelessness. One study finds that being evicted increases the chance of a household using a homeless shelter by 19 percentage points in the following year.6 This represents 304 households or 679 individuals removed from the shelter system. In 2023, the average length of stay in Portland shelters in 2023 was 64 nights,7 and the cost per bednight is currently around $95.8 679 individuals represent 43,456 avoided bed-nights, or a savings of $4,128,320.
Public Education Costs
Maine K-12 schools receive federal assistance to help homeless students through the McKinney-Vento program based on a formula related to their total Title I funding for lowincome students. As a result, schools do not receive more funding based on the share of their low-income population that is homeless. Reducing the number of homeless students under the EPP will free up more of the McKinney-Vento money to help other homeless students.
In 2025, MaineHousing announced the award of $2 million to support students at risk of homelessness in select Maine school districts. MaineHousing estimated the program could help up to 1,750 students.9 Evictions prevented by the EPPP would reduce the demand on this separate program.
Child Welfare Costs
Children also face fewer instances of abuse and neglect, and are less likely to be placed into foster care or other protective arrangements when their families have supportive housing. One study found that providing housing supports to families with children reduced child welfare costs by $14,600 per family over five years.10 Adjusted for inflation and annualized, this is the equivalent of $3,151 per family per year.11 MaineHousing does not publish data on the number of families with or without children in the EPP, Census Bureau data suggests that 41% of households in poverty in Maine include children.12 This would be equivalent to 656 families in the EPP. On this basis, the EPP avoids $2,067,056 in child welfare costs each year.

Health Care Costs
There is also evidence that evictions increase emergency room and other health care use.13 Medicaid enrollees in New York who faced eviction were more likely to lose Medicaid coverage entirely, but even with this disenrollment effect, average costs per person were $158 per person higher over 6 months in 2017.14 This translates to $375 per person per year in 2024 dollars.15 For the 3,576 impacted individuals in the EPP, this represents a savings to MaineCare of $1,341,000. Of this amount, approximately $965,000 was paid by the federal government, and $375,000 from the general fund).16 This does not include additional costs to hospitals for free care, or costs passed on through higher premiums to private insurance-holders.
Employment and State Tax Costs
The instability caused by evictions often disrupts individuals' ability to fully participate in the labor market. This results in periods of higher unemployment and ultimately lost earnings. One study estimates a net loss of earnings of up to 7 percent after an eviction.17 Unfortunately, while MaineHousing reports data on the total income of households facing eviction, it does not distinguish between earned income (e.g. from employment) and other kinds of income (e.g. from Social Security, TANF, or other safety-net programs). Adjusting the numbers in the New York study for inflation18 suggests an average reduction in earnings of $1,046 per household, or $1,673,600 per year for the entire program population. This, in turn, results in a loss of sales and excise tax revenues to the state of $103,763 per year.19
Criminal Justice System Costs
Housing instability is also associated with more involvement with the criminal justice system. A 2009 Maine study found that access to housing supports reduced the amount of time homeless individuals spent in jail from an average of 4.8 days per person to 0.2 days per person.20 Holding someone in jail in Maine costs approximately $173 per day.21 Accordingly, the EPP saves 16,450 jail-days, at a savings of $2,845,780 per year.

Jonah Fertig-Burd DURHAM LD 1287
Distinguished Chairperson Curry, Representative Gere, and esteemed committee members, I appreciate the opportunity to address you today regarding LD 1287. My name is Jonah Fertig-Burd and I live in Durham. I am farmer and a small business owner, As a concerned resident invested in our state's future prosperity, I stand before you advocating for this essential legislation that addresses the critical connection between housing accessibility and economic vitality in Maine. This bill represents a forward-thinking approach to tackling two interconnected challenges that threaten our communities: workforce shortages and housing insecurity.
Our state faces unprecedented demographic and economic pressures affecting our labor market. Maine experienced a significant workforce contraction during recent years, with approximately 26,000 workers leaving the labor pool during the pandemic. Despite partial recovery, we confront an aging workforce, with retirement-age residents outnumbering younger workers entering the job market. These structural challenges require innovative solutions that both attract new talent to Maine and enable current residents to remain productive members of our economy. Housing instability undermines these efforts, creating barriers to steady employment and community investment.
LD 1287's establishment of dedicated housing stability resources represents a strategic investment in Maine's economic foundation. By preventing displacement and homelessness, this program will generate measurable returns across multiple sectors. Employers will benefit from a more reliable workforce pipeline, while families will gain the security needed to focus on career advancement and community engagement. This approach acknowledges the fundamental reality that housing security is not merely a social service concern but an economic development imperative. Maine's tradition of community-centered problem-solving is embodied in this legislation, which recognizes that our collective prosperity depends on ensuring basic needs are met for all residents.
I respectfully encourage this committee to advance LD 1287 as a prudent and necessary measure that will yield substantial returns on investment. By addressing housing instability proactively, we avoid the substantially higher costs associated with responding to homelessness through emergency services, healthcare interventions, and lost productivity. This legislation represents sound fiscal policy paired with compassionate community values. Supporting stable housing today strengthens Maine's workforce, economic competitiveness, and community resilience for decades to come. Thank you for your thoughtful consideration of this vital initiative that will benefit all Maine communities.

Good morning, esteemed committee members. My name is Marco Sousa and I'm a student here in Maine. I'm here today to speak in support of LD 1287, because even
though I'm still in school, I know what it's like when housing isn't stable, and I know I'm not the only one.

10046455:
Testimony of Meredith Anderson, Scarborough Maine
In Favor of: LD 1451 An Act to Advance Coordination of Community Transportation - Sponsored by Senator Mike Tipping
Submitted April 17, 2025
Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and Honorable Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Transportation:
My name is Meredith Anderson; I am a resident of Scarborough. I work for Southern Maine Agency on Aging. The Southern Maine Agency on Aging is the focal point in Cumberland and York counties for resources, services, and information to empower older adults, adults with disabilities, and their caregivers to live to their fullest potential.
I support LD 1451 and appreciate this legislation being brought forward, highlighting the critical need for increases in accessible transportation and transportation coordination for our state's most vulnerable community members.
We have found transportation to be the pillar of not only aging in place but thriving in place. We receive a multitude of calls each year with varying stories but the same need. In 2024, we received over 331 calls and in the past three years, we have received over 1,220 calls from older adults in Southern Maine who are in need of transportation options and help with navigating the existing systems.
A Resource Specialist at SMAA has been working with a 64-year-old woman who lives alone and faces significant challenges due to isolation and mental health issues. She has no informal support to assist her with transportation needs nor does she have the financial means to own and maintain a car. She relies on the Meals on Wheels (MOW) program for nutrition and uses Modivcare for transportation to medical appointments. Recently, she was enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) to help her be able to afford food. However, she has no means of getting to the grocery store to use this benefit. There are no volunteer transportation network or public transportation options in the remote town where she lives. The combination of financial constraints, isolation, mental health challenges, and lack of transportation creates a complex situation for this community member and so many others. While more towns are providing volunteer transportation options, there is still a big gap in service for the most vulnerable individuals living in rural communities.
Many individuals who reach out to us do not have access to technology and/or cannot afford internet services to be able to navigate transportation systems that may be available. Some older adults have expressed it is difficult to find transportation because they are not able to participate in options that require a phone app. Moreover, there are vulnerable individuals who

are not able to engage with complex systems due to cognitive, emotional or financial challenges and need support from others with navigation. Some older adults have also expressed being worried about being left at an appointment. More coordination and support will help to alleviate the stress for these individuals as well as make a more efficient and streamlined approach.
Many individuals who use a wheelchair and need support walking or waiting for a bus are not able to use current transportation options and even make it to a doctor's office. Some transportation supports are only available for medical appointments, meaning these individuals aren't able to go to the pharmacy to pick up their prescriptions, get groceries, go to the bank or post office, go to the Social Security Office or DHHS office, if needed. Not only are people not able to run simple errands to maintain their household, but they are also not able to participate in social activities. There is no access to transportation to church, a dinner, or coffee with a friend. Slowly, not only the circle of support dwindles, but so too does an individual's physical, mental and emotional health.
Access to reliable transportation enhances the overall well-being for older adults and helps individuals to remain living in the community longer. 87% of adults over 45 say that it is important to be able to stay in their own home as they get older. Thriving in our communities is the goal for so many of us; having access to transportation is essential to realizing that goal. Having mobility management hubs will provide better service and support for all residents. And what's more, the state can save a tremendous amount when older adults stay home and are not living in long-term care facilities before this level of support is truly needed.
Thank you for reading this testimony and for your consideration of an ought to pass vote for improving access to transportation and the well-being of our community members.
Meredith Anderson, LCSW

Committee on Housing and Economic Development: I am Senator Rick Bennett of Oxford, and I have the honor of serving 14 communities in Western Maine in the State Senate. I am proud to cosponsor LD 1287, "An Act to Support Workforce Development by Establishing
the Housing Stability Fund."
LD 1287 will provide targeted rental assistance and housing stability for Maine's most
vulnerable residents. This thoughtful and impactful legislation not only addresses the immediate needs of low-income households but also aligns with Maine's long-term economic and community development goals.

By offering up to $3,000 in rental assistance to households earning less than 30% of the
area median income, this bill will reach a population often overlooked by traditional housing programs. These residents are at the highest risk of eviction and housing insecurity, and this assistance would make a real and immediate difference in their lives. Preventing eviction is more than a compassionate step, it is a proactive investment in the health and stability of
our communities.

Furthermore, there is a clear connection between housing and employment. Stable housing provides the foundation individuals need to maintain jobs and participate fully in the
workforce. This legislation supports Maine workers, particularly those in essential roles who
too often face housing challenges despite their contributions to the state's economy.

LD 1287 also demonstrates a commitment to responsible and localized program
administration. With the Maine State Housing Authority working alongside trusted community organizations, assistance will be delivered efficiently and effectively by those
who understand the unique needs of their regions. A cap of 10% on administrative costs
ensures the vast majority of funds go directly to renters.

Moreover, this program has already shown success across different parts of the state. In
Southern Maine, security deposit assistance has helped stabilize housing, while in Androscoggin County, supplemental rent support has proven to be effective. These localized strategies have strengthened communities, supported local economies, and reduced reliance
on public services.

I urge you to support the passage of this bill. It is a practical, compassionate, and fiscally sound response to Maine's housing challenges, and will have a lasting, positive impact on individuals, families, and communities across the state.

Testimony in Support of LD 1287
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and Members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee,
My name is Robby Perkins-High, and I work as the Director of Housing Initiatives for ProsperityME. I also serve on Portland's CDBG Allocation Committee and as a Board Member for Ketcha Outdoors, and am a resident of Portland.
I write to you today in support of LD 1287, a bill that will provide housing stabilization for Maine's most vulnerable renters. This policy is both fiscally and morally sound, and would provide a crucial source of funding to address Maine's housing crisis.
From a financial perspective, a 2025 Shelter Cost study from MaineHousing estimated that the minimum cost of a family shelter bed in the state was $17,583 per year, with some areas of the state seeing significantly higher costs. This program would limit assistance to $3,000 per household, which would be leveraged to allow families to stay in their current housing. With minimal financial support, the state can support the most aXordable method of addressing homelessness: preventing it from happening in the first place. The bill also limits administrative costs to 10%, meaning that almost all of this investment will flow to the people who need it the most, adding to the eXiciency of the program.
Outcomes from ProsperityME's prior work show how eXective this program can be. In pilot work with similar funding, the average length of support needed was just four months before clients became self-suXicient. Of all clients served, there were none that came back for additional funding. This is not a program that people will rely on in the long-term to pay their bills, or one where the problem will persist after their participation. This is a small amount of support that allows families and individuals to keep things on track when something knocks them oX course.
I urge the committee to vote in favor of this program that will keep Mainers housed, in a cost-eXective way for the state, allowing them to continue to contribute to their communities.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Joshua J. Reny Assistant City Manager
April 24, 2025
Housing and Economic Development Committee Cross Building, Room 206 Augusta, ME 04333
Re: Support of LD 1287
Dear Sen. Curry, Rep. Gere, and Housing and Economic Development Committee Members:
My name is Scott Morelli, and as City Manager for South Portland, I am testifying today in SUPPORT of LD 1287: An Act to Support Workforce Development by Establishing the Housing Stability Fund.
In these uncertain economic times, housing affordability is one thing that remains a certainty. Attracting and retaining workers in both the public and private sectors also remains a definite challenge. LD 1287 offers a solution to both of these issues.
This legislation provides the Maine State Housing Authority (MSHA) with $1.9 million annually to distribute to area agencies who will in turn use those funds to help best meet the housing needs of vulnerable residents in their communities. These funds would target households earning less than 30% of the area median income by providing up to $3,000 in rental assistance, thus helping to prevent homelessness and housing instability. This could include assistance with security deposits, which can be a barrier to obtaining housing, or supplemental rental assistance, which helps keep families in homes.
Data suggests that those with secure housing are more apt to maintain employment and workforce participation than those who are unhoused. By helping people secure or maintain their housing, we help secure and maintain their presence in the workforce, so that they can eventually move up and no longer need assistance. Allowing these vulnerable residents to be evicted, on the other hand, causes a whole host of problems. They now need shelter, which are expensive to operate, and being unhoused can result in dropping out of the workforce, thus making these individuals in need of more financial assistance from the State and local government.
This is also a program that is proven to work. Between 2023 and 2024, a total of 240 lowincome households in Southern Maine received help with security deposits, and 109 families accessed short-term rental assistance to serve as a steppingstone to employment and selfsufficiency--using an average of just 4 months of support. So rather than remaining unhoused or being evicted, these 240 households received a few months of support, avoided being unhoused, and were successful members of Maine's workforce, providing needed labor to Maine businesses.

Testimony of The Maine Real Estate Managers Association
TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT OF LD 1287 -- "AN ACT TO SUPPORT WORKFORCE HOUSING BY ESTABLISHING THE HOUSING STABILITY FUND"
Tuesday, April 23, 2025
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and the esteemed members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development. My name is Sherrin Vail, and I am speaking on behalf of the Maine Real Estate Manager's Association. We support LD 1287, An Act to Support Workforce Development by Establishing the Housing Stability Fund, because this bill
will provide funding to a vulnerable population of those that make less than 30% area median income. It will provide housing stability for those unable to receive a Section 8 voucher to support higher rents due to the extended or closed
waitlists in Maine.
Our member property management companies provide affordable housing for those in need across the state of Maine. It is important to us that our residents are afforded every opportunity to maintain their housing, despite increasing costs
for food, gas, utilities and everyday life expenses. By providing rare support for this demographic of renters, the program aims to reduce homelessness and housing instability, which are critical factors in workforce retention and
community well-being.
Supporting LD 1287 is an investment in Maine's workforce and communities. By providing targeted rental and security deposit assistance to those most in need, the bill promotes economic stability, reduces homelessness, and strengthens
the state's long-term economic health.
I urge you to support LD 1287 and invest in a program that strengthens communities and most importantly, keeps Mainers in their homes.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely, Sherrin Vail, Maine Real Estate Manager's Association
